title: Coppersmith’s Method (Idea) — Small Roots Mod N (Toy)

questions.question: What does it mean for x0 to be a root of f(x) modulo N?
options: f(x0) ≡ 0 (mod N)
f(x0) = 0 over the reals only
f(x0) is prime
x0 divides N
questions.explanation: A modular root satisfies f(x0) mod N = 0.

questions.question: Why is a “small unknown” in a structured RSA plaintext a red flag?
options: It can sometimes be modeled as a small root of a modular polynomial
It always makes RSA decryption faster
It prevents padding oracles
It forces N to be composite
questions.explanation: Small unknowns can be targeted by small-root techniques when a polynomial can be constructed.

questions.question: In the stereotyped-message setup c ≡ (m0 + x)^e (mod N), what is the attacker trying to recover?
options: The small x
The primes p and q directly
The public exponent e
The hash function used in OAEP
questions.explanation: x is the hidden “small” part; once x is known, m is known.

questions.question: What makes Coppersmith’s method different from brute forcing x?
options: It uses lattice reduction to find small roots efficiently without trying all x
It requires guessing the private key first
It works only when x is large
It replaces RSA with ECC
questions.explanation: Brute force is exponential in x size; Coppersmith uses lattices to do better under bounds.

questions.question: Why are small public exponents (like e=3) often mentioned in small-root RSA attacks?
options: They produce lower-degree polynomials, which can make small-root recovery easier
They make RSA unkeyed
They eliminate the need for padding
They prevent any lattice construction
questions.explanation: Lower-degree polynomials can improve the feasibility of small-root methods.

questions.question: Which mitigation best addresses “structured plaintext + RSA” risks in real systems?
options: Use standardized randomized padding/KEM constructions (e.g., OAEP / hybrid)
Use a fixed plaintext header
Use shorter keys to reduce computation
Use hex encoding for plaintexts
questions.explanation: Randomized padding/KEM breaks the attacker’s ability to build a predictable polynomial.

questions.question: What is the key requirement for small-root recovery to be possible?
options: The root must be sufficiently small relative to N and the polynomial degree
N must be prime
The attacker must know the private exponent d
The ciphertext must be ASCII
questions.explanation: Coppersmith-style results require bounds on root size vs modulus and degree.

questions.question: Why is brute forcing x not a realistic attack on properly sized RSA in practice?
options: Because x is typically too large (many bits), making exhaustive search infeasible
Because brute force requires factoring N first
Because brute force cannot evaluate polynomials modulo N
Because brute force only works on elliptic curves
questions.explanation: Brute force scales with the size of x; real unknowns are far too large to enumerate.
